stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.1 key concept: Song China combined an examination-based bureaucracy, Neo-Confucianism, and commercial growth
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing government and economy in Song China, 960–1279
stimulusBlocks.text:
Song China (960–1279) governed through a large civil service. Officials were chosen by examinations on Confucian texts, and a successful candidate could rise regardless of birth, although the long years of study favored families that could afford teachers. Neo-Confucian scholars revived Confucian ideas about duty and self-cultivation, which shaped education.

The economy grew quickly. Farmers planted fast-ripening Champa rice, introduced from Southeast Asia, which allowed two harvests a year in some regions. Printing spread books and examination texts, and by the 1100s the government issued paper money. Foot binding, which spread among elite families during the Song, limited the mobility of many women.

questions.explanation: Fast-ripening rice allowed more food per year, supporting more people and trade.
choiceExplanations: Fast-ripening rice allowed more food per year, supporting more people and trade.
Paper money and rice were separate developments, and the passage connects rice to harvests.
The passage does not say rice reduced taxes.
The passage describes domestic growth and not grain exports to Europe.
questions.distinguisher: Song trade did expand, but the passage ties rice directly to farming output.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Marco Polo, Venetian merchant who traveled in Mongol-ruled Asia c. 1271–1295, account dictated to the writer Rustichello of Pisa, c. 1298, describing Yuan China
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Book of Ser Marco Polo, trans. Henry Yule, rev. Henri Cordier, 3rd ed. (London: John Murray, 1903), vol. 1, Book II, ch. 26. Project Gutenberg eBook #10636.
stimulusBlocks.note: Cambaluc was the Yuan capital, present-day Beijing. “Yamb” is a version of the Mongol word yam.
stimulusBlocks.text:
And the messengers of the Emperor in travelling from Cambaluc, be the road whichsoever they will, find at every twenty-five miles of the journey a station which they call Yamb, or, as we should say, the "Horse-Post-House." . . . The passage itself says communities had to supply horses, so the burden was real even if it was not paid from the treasury.
No evidence shows the emperor ordered his description.

questions.distinguisher: Historians debate how much of China Polo saw, but the problem here is how he described the costs of the system.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.1 key concept: gunpowder weapons helped the Ottomans conquer Constantinople and build a multiethnic empire
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople, 1453
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire, with a large army and powerful cannon, including bronze guns cast by a Hungarian engineer named Urban. The city's walls had held for a thousand years, but they could not withstand sustained bombardment, and the Ottomans took the city on May 29.

Mehmed made it his capital, now called Istanbul, rebuilt its markets and population, and converted the Hagia Sophia from a church into a mosque. He allowed the Greek Orthodox patriarch to remain in office, and he encouraged Greeks, Jews, and Armenians to settle in the city.

The passage describes rebuilding the city as the sultan's capital.
questions.distinguisher: Mehmed did convert Hagia Sophia, but he did not require conversion of the population.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing architecture in land-based empires, c. 1550–1700
stimulusBlocks.text:
Land-based empires used architecture to display their power and faith. The Ottoman architect Sinan designed the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul, completed in 1557 for Suleiman I, with a vast central dome and four minarets. In Persia, Shah Abbas I made Isfahan his capital in 1598 and rebuilt it with a great public square and the Imam Mosque, covered in colored tile.

In India, the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in the 1630s and 1640s as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Built of white marble, it combined Persian, Islamic, and Indian decorative traditions. In China, the Qing emperors maintained and expanded the Forbidden City in Beijing as the center of imperial ceremony.

In 1938 British prime minister Neville Chamberlain and French premier Édouard Daladier agreed at Munich to let Germany annex the Sudetenland, a border region of Czechoslovakia, in the hope of avoiding war. For decades after 1945, many writers condemned the policy of appeasement as a failure of nerve that encouraged Hitler to demand more. Germany occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939 and invaded Poland in September.

Some historians now argue that Britain and France had good reasons to avoid war in 1938. Their armies were not ready, public opinion in Britain and in the empire opposed another war so soon after 1918, and the Munich agreement gave them time to rearm. Other historians reply that Germany was relatively weaker in 1938 than it would be later, so waiting did not help the Allies.

parts.prompt: Identify ONE argument the passage presents in defense of the policy of appeasement.
criteria: States a specific argument from the passage.
Connects it to avoiding or delaying war in 1938.

model.answer: Some historians argue that Britain and France were not ready for war in 1938.
model.prove: The passage says their armies were not ready and that the Munich agreement gave them time to rearm.
model.explain: If the Allies lacked the strength to win quickly, accepting a settlement could be a way to prepare for a later war.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also identify the argument that public opinion in Britain and the empire opposed another war so soon after 1918.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE piece of historical evidence, not mentioned in the passage, that supports the argument that Hitler's goals were not limited to the Sudetenland.
criteria: Gives a specific example beyond the passage.
Explains how it shows aggressive aims beyond the Sudetenland.

model.answer: Germany had already taken other territory in violation of the Treaty of Versailles.
model.prove: Hitler sent troops into the demilitarized Rhineland in 1936 and annexed Austria in the Anschluss of March 1938.
model.explain: Each success strengthened Germany's position and showed that Hitler was willing to break the treaty and expand when the Allies did not resist.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain Hitler's occupation of Prague in March 1939, which broke the Munich agreement, or his statement of the need for living space in the east.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE way the policy of appeasement affected relations between the Western powers and the Soviet Union.
criteria: Names a specific event or decision.
Explains how appeasement shaped Soviet policy or Western–Soviet relations.

model.answer: Appeasement increased Soviet distrust of Britain and France.
model.prove: The Soviet Union was not invited to the Munich conference in 1938, and in August 1939 Stalin signed a nonaggression pact with Germany.
model.explain: Stalin concluded that the Western powers hoped to turn Germany eastward, so he made an agreement that bought time and allowed Germany to invade Poland.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain that the failure of appeasement led Britain and France to guarantee Poland's independence in 1939, which brought them into war when Germany invaded.

stimulusBlocks.source: montaigne-cotton-1877
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Michel de Montaigne, French writer and landowner, essay “Of Cannibals,” published in 1580, discussing the Tupinamba people of Brazil
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Essays of Montaigne, trans. Charles Cotton, ed. William Carew Hazlitt (1877), Book I, ch. 30, “Of Cannibals.” Project Gutenberg eBook #3600.
stimulusBlocks.note: Antarctic France was a short-lived French colony in Brazil founded by Villegaignon in 1555. “This nation” means the Tupinamba. The last lines refer to cruelty during France's wars of religion.
stimulusBlocks.text:
I long had a man in my house that lived ten or twelve years in the New World, discovered in these latter days, and in that part of it where Villegaignon landed, . . . which he called Antarctic France. . . .

Now, to return to my subject, I find that there is nothing barbarous and savage in this nation, by anything that I can gather, excepting, that every one gives the title of barbarism to everything that is not in use in his own country. . . .

I am not sorry that we should here take notice of the barbarous horror of so cruel an action, but that, seeing so clearly into their faults, we should be so blind to our own. I conceive there is more barbarity in eating a man alive, than when he is dead; in tearing a body limb from limb by racks and torments, that is yet in perfect sense; . . . (as we have not only read, but lately seen, not amongst inveterate and mortal enemies, but among neighbours and fellow-citizens, and, which is worse, under colour of piety and religion), than to roast and eat him after he is dead.

model.answer: Montaigne claims that people call barbaric whatever is not the custom in their own country.
model.prove: He writes that “every one gives the title of barbarism to everything that is not in use in his own country.”
model.explain: The claim suggests that European judgments of Indigenous Americans reflected habit and bias more than a fair comparison.

model.answer: Montaigne wrote during the French wars of religion and used the Tupinamba to criticize Europeans.
model.prove: He compares the cruelty of eating a dead enemy with the torture and killing of neighbors “under colour of piety and religion” in France.
model.explain: Because his purpose was to criticize his own society, the passage is strong evidence of one French thinker's views but may idealize the Tupinamba and cannot be treated as a full account of their lives.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also note that Montaigne relied on a servant who had lived in Brazil rather than on his own observation.

model.answer: Some Spanish writers and officials argued that Indigenous peoples should be treated more humanely.
model.prove: The priest Bartolomé de las Casas criticized the encomienda system and the abuse of Indigenous workers, and the Spanish crown issued the New Laws of 1542 to limit forced labor.
model.explain: The debate shows that some Europeans questioned conquest and forced labor, though the reforms were often poorly enforced.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain the Valladolid debate of 1550 and 1551 between Las Casas and Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda over the rights of Indigenous peoples.

parts.prompt: Identify ONE way rulers of Song China chose officials for their government.
criteria: Names a specific method or institution.

model.answer: Song rulers chose many officials through civil service examinations.
model.prove: Candidates studied Confucian classics and took written examinations, and successful candidates received posts in the imperial bureaucracy.
model.explain: The examinations let the emperor recruit educated officials whose careers depended on the central government instead of on aristocratic birth alone.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also identify the use of recommendations from officials or the use of examination degrees to rank officials.

parts.prompt: Describe ONE way political authority in feudal Western Europe differed from political authority in Song China.
criteria: Describes a specific feature of European authority.
Makes the difference from Song China clear.

model.answer: Power in Western Europe was divided among kings, nobles, and the Church instead of being centralized in a bureaucracy.
model.prove: Kings depended on lords who held land in return for military service, and the lords' own vassals owed loyalty to them, so a king could not directly command all his subjects.
model.explain: Song emperors ruled through officials who answered to the court, so European rulers had less direct control over their territories.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also describe manorialism, in which lords controlled the labor of serfs, or the weakness of royal tax systems compared with Song revenues.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE way the Catholic Church influenced political authority in Western Europe between 1200 and 1450.
criteria: Names a specific action, institution, or conflict.
Explains how it affected rulers or their power.

model.answer: The Church could pressure rulers by threatening spiritual penalties.
model.prove: Pope Innocent III placed England under an interdict and excommunicated King John, and in 1213 John submitted and accepted the pope as his feudal lord.
model.explain: Because most people believed these penalties affected their salvation, rulers who angered the pope risked losing support from their subjects.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain that the Church crowned kings and emperors, ran courts under canon law, or collected tithes that gave it wealth independent of rulers.

documents.label: “All Power to the Soviets!”
documents.attribution: John Reed, American journalist and socialist who witnessed the Russian Revolution in Petrograd, Ten Days That Shook the World, 1919
documents.content:
In this atmosphere of corruption, of monstrous half-truths, one clear note sounded day after day, the deepening chorus of the Bolsheviki, "All Power to the Soviets! All power to the direct representatives of millions on millions of common workers, soldiers, peasants. Land, bread, an end to the senseless war, an end to secret diplomacy, speculation, treachery. . . . The Revolution is in danger, and with it the cause of the people all over the world!" . . .

Week by week food became scarcer. The daily allowance of bread fell from a pound and a half to a pound, then three quarters, half, and a quarter-pound. Toward the end there was a week without any bread at all.
documents.citation: John Reed, Ten Days That Shook the World (1919), ch. 1. Project Gutenberg eBook #3076.
documents.note: The Bolsheviki were the Bolsheviks, led by Lenin. Soviets were councils of workers and soldiers. The Provisional Government ruled Russia between the tsar's abdication in March 1917 and the Bolshevik seizure of power in November 1917. The ellipsis after “treachery” appears in Reed's own text.

If we aim deliberately at the impoverishment of Central Europe, vengeance, I dare predict, will not limp. Nothing can then delay for very long that final civil war between the forces of Reaction and the despairing convulsions of Revolution, before which the horrors of the late German war will fade into nothing . . . .

Communism is based on the belief that man is so weak and inadequate that he is unable to govern himself, and therefore requires the rule of strong masters.

options.modelResponse:
In 1900, most governments played a limited role in daily economic life, but the First World War, the Russian Revolution, and the Great Depression led many people to ask whether governments should take on much more. The Cold War then divided the world between states with market economies and states with planned economies, and the late twentieth century produced new debates about markets and regulation.

Between 1917 and 2000, ideas about the role of government changed substantially, moving from confidence in an active state in the early and middle decades toward greater trust in markets after 1980, but the shift was incomplete because governments continued to regulate, to set rules for trade, and to defend political systems.

In the first half of the century, many writers expected governments to act. In Petrograd, the Bolsheviks called for "All Power to the Soviets" and promised land, bread, and peace as the Provisional Government failed to feed the city (Document 1). John Reed, an American socialist who supported the revolution, had reason to highlight the Bolsheviks' appeal, but his description of falling bread rations helps explain why many Russians turned to a government that promised to take control of the economy. After the war, Keynes warned that the Treaty of Versailles had "no provisions for the economic rehabilitation of Europe" and predicted revolution if Central Europe were impoverished (Document 2). Writing after resigning from the British delegation, Keynes wanted to persuade readers that governments had a responsibility to plan for recovery. The Great Depression and the New Deal in the United States confirmed this view: governments took on responsibility for employment and relief.

During the Cold War, the debate was about which kind of government should rule. President Truman described communism as based on the belief that people need "strong masters," while democracy rested on the "capacity . . . to govern himself" (Document 3). Speaking in 1949 during the Berlin airlift, Truman had a purpose of rallying Americans and allies behind containment, so his contrast is stark. Yet he did not oppose government action: the Marshall Plan committed billions of dollars in public aid to rebuild Western Europe. Nixon's 1970 call for "comprehensive new regulations" on pollution (Document 4) shows that active government remained a mainstream view in a Republican administration, and he used it to respond to growing public concern and the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency.

After 1975, confidence in the state declined. Reagan said that "government is not the solution to our problem" and proposed to remove "roadblocks" to the economy (Document 5). He spoke after a decade of inflation and slow growth, and his inaugural address was meant to justify tax cuts and deregulation. Similar ideas shaped Margaret Thatcher's privatizations in Britain and the market reforms of Deng Xiaoping in China. The collapse of communist governments in 1989, celebrated by Bush (Document 6), seemed to confirm the failure of central planning, though Bush was also claiming credit for his country's Cold War policy. Gorbachev's perestroika and glasnost had opened the way.

By 2000, the debate had shifted again. Clinton described globalization as "the central reality of our time" and urged "rule-based trade" that would not tolerate "a race to the bottom" in the environment and worker protection (Document 7). Speaking soon after the protests at the WTO meeting in Seattle, he had a political reason to show that he took critics seriously. His position shows that even leaders who praised markets accepted a role for government in setting rules.

In conclusion, ideas about government moved from confidence in state direction to greater trust in markets, but governments never stopped regulating, protecting, and setting the terms of exchange, so the change was real but incomplete.

options.modelResponse:
Before 1500, China had the world's largest economy and a history of foreign trade, but the Ming dynasty, founded in 1368, restricted private overseas trade after the voyages of Zheng He ended in the 1430s. Government revenue came mainly from land taxes collected from peasants, and the Confucian civil service examinations selected officials.

Between 1500 and 1750, global trade changed China's economy significantly by bringing in silver and new crops, but it did not change the Confucian state or the dominance of agriculture, so the change was major in the economy and limited in politics and social order.

The flow of silver reshaped the economy. After the Spanish founded Manila in 1571, galleons carried silver from the Americas across the Pacific, and Chinese merchants exchanged silk and porcelain for it. China's demand for silver was strong because the Ming government, in tax reforms often called the Single Whip, collected taxes in silver. As a result, markets expanded, more peasants sold crops and crafts for money, and cities such as Jingdezhen grew as centers of porcelain production for export.

New crops from the Americas also changed society. Maize, sweet potatoes, and peanuts could grow on hillsides and poor soil, and historians connect them to the growth of China's population in the 1600s and 1700s. More people settled in upland areas, which changed the landscape and farming.

However, important structures stayed the same. The Confucian examination system and the emperor's authority continued under both the Ming and the Qing, who took power in 1644. Most people remained peasant farmers, family and kinship stayed central, and the court still limited foreign merchants to certain ports and did not give them political influence. Silver also showed China's vulnerability: when imports declined in the 1630s and 1640s, the shortage of silver contributed to a fiscal crisis that helped bring down the Ming.

In conclusion, global trade transformed money, markets, and food in China, but the political system and the central role of agriculture remained, so the change was deep in the economy and shallow in the structure of the state.

modelNotes.text: The first paragraph describes the Ming dynasty, the end of Zheng He's voyages, and China's tax system before 1500.

modelNotes.label: Thesis
modelNotes.text: The thesis answers the question of extent, distinguishing change in the economy from continuity in politics and social order.

modelNotes.label: Evidence
modelNotes.text: Manila, silver taxation, Jingdezhen, new American crops, the examination system, and the Ming fiscal crisis are specific and used to support the argument.

modelNotes.label: Analysis and reasoning
modelNotes.text: The essay organizes evidence around what changed and what continued, and it qualifies the claim by noting China's vulnerability to changes in the silver supply.

options.alternateModel: A different strong essay could argue that global trade changed China less than it changed the Americas or Europe, using the Qing's control of foreign merchants and the small share of trade in China's economy as evidence of continuity.
commonErrors: Describing trade without saying how much it changed China.
Claiming that China was isolated from the world before 1500 or after.
Listing changes without any evidence of what stayed the same.
Using events after 1750 as the main evidence.

options.modelResponse:
In 1750, most British workers lived in villages, working in agriculture or at home on goods such as cloth. Families set their own pace of work according to the seasons and daylight. Then new machines, steam engines, and factories began to change how goods were made, starting with cotton textiles in the late 1700s.

Industrialization changed workers' lives greatly in where, when, and how they worked and in their health and political rights, but poverty, long hours, and unequal treatment of women persisted for much of the period, so the change was profound but uneven.

The workplace itself changed. Mechanized cotton mills in Lancashire required workers to follow the schedule of the factory bell and work 12 to 16 hours a day, and the spinning jenny and power loom replaced much of the skilled hand work of artisans. Workers moved to cities such as Manchester, whose population multiplied in the first half of the century. Living conditions in crowded neighborhoods were poor, and cholera epidemics in the 1830s and 1840s killed thousands.

Workers also gained new ways to improve their position. They formed trade unions, which Parliament had banned under the Combination Acts of 1799 but legalized in 1824 and protected by law in 1871. Reformers passed laws such as the Factory Act of 1833, which limited children's hours, and the Mines Act of 1842, which barred women and young children from underground work. The Reform Acts of 1832 and 1867 widened the vote and brought some working men into politics. By the 1870s and 1880s, real wages had risen for many workers.

Yet there were important continuities. Many people still worked in agriculture or in domestic service, which was the largest occupation for women. Women and children continued to earn less than men and did long hours in textile mills and workshops. Poverty remained widespread, and as late as the 1880s surveys found that a large part of London's population lived near subsistence.

In conclusion, industrialization transformed the setting and rhythm of work and eventually gave workers more rights and wages, but poverty and inequality continued, so the change was great in structure and gradual in improvement.

modelNotes.label: Contextualization
modelNotes.text: The first paragraph describes agricultural and household work before industrialization and the start of factory production.

modelNotes.label: Thesis
modelNotes.text: The thesis answers the extent question and previews both change and continuity.

modelNotes.label: Evidence
modelNotes.text: The factory bell, Manchester, cholera, the Combination Acts, the Factory Act of 1833, the Mines Act of 1842, and the Reform Acts are specific and tied to the claim.

modelNotes.label: Analysis and reasoning
modelNotes.text: The essay organizes change and continuity, shows that improvement came gradually, and qualifies the argument by noting uneven effects on women, children, and the poor.

options.alternateModel: A different strong essay could argue that the changes in workers' lives were limited before 1850 and larger afterward, using reform laws and rising wages in the second half of the century as the main turning point.
commonErrors: Describing the Industrial Revolution generally without focusing on workers.
Claiming that all workers lived in factories or cities by 1800.
Listing reforms without explaining how they changed daily life.
Treating Britain's experience as identical to industrialization elsewhere.

options.modelResponse:
By 1900, steamships, railroads, and the telegraph had already linked many parts of the world. Submarine cables connected continents, and the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 had shortened routes between Europe and Asia. These earlier technologies had helped European empires and global trade grow.

Between 1900 and 2001, new technologies of communication and transport greatly increased the speed, volume, and reach of global connections, but political barriers, economic inequality, and the dominance of a few powerful states limited how equally people shared in those connections.

Technology changed the speed and scale of exchange. Commercial jet travel, which began in the late 1950s, cut the time to cross oceans from days to hours and allowed millions of people to travel and migrate. Shipping containers, introduced in the 1950s, lowered the cost of moving goods and made it practical for manufacturers to assemble products using parts from many countries. Radio and television spread news, music, and sports to mass audiences, and the Internet and the World Wide Web, which became widely used in the 1990s, let people exchange information instantly across borders.

Technology also changed the way people experienced events. In 1969 an estimated hundreds of millions of people watched the Apollo moon landing on television, and satellite broadcasts allowed global audiences to watch events as they happened. Disease and finance also moved faster: HIV spread along air routes and migration, and financial crises such as the Asian financial crisis of 1997 spread quickly across markets.

However, important continuities limited these changes. Political divisions shaped the use of technology: during the Cold War, the Iron Curtain and the Berlin Wall restricted travel and information between East and West, and governments such as China's censored the Internet. Economic inequality meant that many people in poorer countries had little access to telephones, computers, or air travel, a gap often called the digital divide. Wealthy industrialized states and their companies also controlled most of the trade and information flows, so technology did not end older patterns of dependence.

In conclusion, technology made global connections faster and broader than ever before, but its benefits were uneven and shaped by governments and economic power, so the change was dramatic in speed and unequal in effect.

modelNotes.text: The first paragraph describes steamships, railroads, the telegraph, and the Suez Canal before 1900.

modelNotes.label: Thesis
modelNotes.text: The thesis answers the question of extent and names both the changes and the limits.

modelNotes.label: Evidence
modelNotes.text: Jet travel, containers, television, the Apollo landing, the Internet, the Cold War barriers, and censorship are specific and used to support both change and continuity.

modelNotes.label: Analysis and reasoning
modelNotes.text: The essay organizes continuity and change and qualifies the claim by showing how politics and inequality limited the effects of technology.

options.alternateModel: A different strong essay could argue that technology changed global connections more before 1950 than after, using the telegraph, steamship, and radio as the main turning points and treating jets and the Internet as extensions.
commonErrors: Listing technologies without explaining how they changed connections.
Treating globalization as new in the twentieth century instead of building on earlier networks.
Ignoring evidence of continuity, such as unequal access and political barriers.
Using developments after 2001 as the main evidence.
